Classic TAM-1 pathway pairing. Together they confer high-level zidovudine resistance and erode tenofovir and abacavir activity.
TAM-2 pathway pairing that frequently co-occurs with K70R, forming a distinct resistance trajectory from the TAM-1 route.
Common TAM-2 accessory pair; individually modest but additive when combined, reducing zidovudine and tenofovir susceptibility.
Frequent co-occurrence on the TAM-1 trajectory; associated with pronounced thymidine analogue resistance.
Key TAM-1 core doublet; strongly associated with tenofovir cross-resistance when present alongside T215Y.
High-level TAM-1 anchor combination causing severe reduction in AZT and d4T efficacy.
M184V partially resensitizes the virus to tenofovir in the presence of K65R, representing an important within-class antagonism.
Often selected together under abacavir/lamivudine regimens; M184V mitigates viral fitness costs caused by L74V.
A62V is a key accessory component of the Q151M multi-drug resistance complex, amplifying broad NRTI resistance.
Co-occurrence reflects sequential NNRTI therapy failures, conferring total resistance to first-generation NNRTIs.
P225H almost exclusively arises in combination with K103N under Efavirenz pressure, reinforcing high-level NNRTI resistance.
Combines Nevirapine-selected Y181C with Efavirenz-selected G190A, eliminating options across 1st generation NNRTIs.
L100I and K103N act synergistically to increase Efavirenz resistance over 1,000-fold compared to wildtype.
G140S is an accessory mutation that restores viral fitness lost to Q148 mutations and amplifies resistance to raltegravir and dolutegravir.
Same compensatory relationship as Q148H/G140S; one of the most clinically important INSTI resistance signatures.
E138K is a secondary INSTI mutation that, alongside Q148 substitutions, contributes to a stepwise increase in INSTI resistance.
Represents two distinct INSTI resistance pathways found in the same profile, suggesting dual exposure or mixed viral populations.
Triple-combo component with Q148H; creates near complete cross-resistance to first and second generation INSTIs.
Typically arise on separate resistance pathways; co-occurrence suggests multi-pathway protease inhibitor pressure.
